raw_response:
I'm 62 this year, and I've been farming these 12 mu in Quzhou County for 45 years. I studied at the agricultural college back in the day, so I understand the science behind soil nutrients and crop physiology, but my farm is only 12 mu — that makes me a smallholder no matter how much I know. With just my wife and me working the land, cash and labor are always tight. The children are off working in Shijiazhuang, so we hire help when we have to, but every yuan spent on hired labor is a yuan I can't spend on fertilizer.

My land is split between two systems. I keep 8 mu in the wheat-maize double crop — it's the backbone of our food security and provides steady grain income. The other 4 mu I plant to cotton. I know cotton is labor-intensive, especially the picking, but the cash return per mu is better than maize when prices are decent, and diversifying means if one crop fails, we still have something.

For the winter wheat on the 8 mu, I'll plant around October 8th, right after National Day. I'm using Jinmai 47 — I know the seed, it performs consistently on this loam soil. I'm targeting 18 kg N per mu this year. The soil test from last spring showed medium fertility, and the extension recommendation would be 20 kg N for a 500 kg/mu yield target, but fertilizer prices are up and I need to keep some cash in reserve. I'll split it: 10 kg N as base dressing using compound fertilizer before planting, then 8 kg urea at jointing stage in late March. I'll irrigate three times — pre-winter, jointing, and grain filling — at about 40 yuan per mu per irrigation. Pumping water is expensive, but on the North China Plain, wheat without irrigation is a gamble I can't afford. I'm expecting about 460 kg/mu.

The summer maize turnaround is always brutal — usually only five or six days between wheat harvest and maize planting in mid-June. I'll plant Zhengdan 958 immediately after the combine leaves the field. With maize, there's no time for fancy split applications, so I'll put down 16 kg N per mu all at planting, plus some phosphorus and potassium. If the July rains come normally, I'll irrigate twice; if it's dry, three times. Target yield is 500 kg/mu, though that depends heavily on August rainfall.

For cotton on the 4 mu, I'll plant in late April. I'm using a hybrid variety — the seed cost is higher, but the vigor matters for early establishment. I'll apply 14 kg N per mu, split between base dressing and flowering stage. Cotton needs careful water management, so I'll irrigate twice: once at flowering and once at boll development. Too much water and the bolls drop; too little and the fiber quality suffers. I'm targeting 270 kg lint per mu. I know I could push for 300 kg with more fertilizer, but at my age and with only two of us, I'd rather be conservative than risk losing money on inputs.

Labor is my biggest constraint. For wheat and maize, my wife and I can handle most of the work, but wheat harvest and maize planting in that narrow window will require hired labor — probably 4 days total across the two crops, plus custom combining. Cotton is where the labor really piles up: planting, thinning, pest scouting, and especially picking in September and October. I'll need about 10 days of hired labor for cotton across the season. Family labor will be roughly 40 days for wheat, 25 for maize, and 45 for cotton — my wife and I spread it out, but at 62, I feel the physical limits more each year.
